summary: The Peer-to-Peer Streaming Tracker Protocol is an application-layer signaling protocol for exchanging meta information between trackers and peers. This standards-track RFC specifies version 1: architecture, message flows, formats and syntax. It lets cooperating peers form a network for streaming.

eli5.summary: Viewers helping each other get a video, with a directory service that tells each one who else is watching so they can share.

questions: what is a tracker in peer to peer streaming

subtitle: How peers in a peer-to-peer video stream find each other by asking a tracker over HTTP and JSON.

tldr.problem: Peers that share live or on-demand media with each other need a standard way to join a group, learn who else is in it, and report how they are doing.
tldr.mechanism: PPSTP defines three JSON requests (CONNECT, FIND, STAT_REPORT) that a peer sends to a tracker with HTTP POST. The tracker answers each one with a response, which can carry a list of other peers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7846 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It carries only signaling: the media itself moves between peers using a separate peer protocol.

today: RFC 7846 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2016, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the Tracker Protocol half of PPSP, paired with the Peer Protocol in RFC 7574.

sections.title: What PPSTP Is For
sections.content:
The Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol (PPSP) has two halves: the Tracker Protocol, defined in RFC 7846, and the Peer Protocol, defined in RFC 7574. RFC 6972 sets the requirements that the Tracker Protocol meets.

The Peer-to-Peer Streaming Tracker Protocol (PPSTP) lets peers send meta information to a tracker, report their streaming status, and get lists of other peers back. A tracker is a directory service for a given audio or video channel or streaming file. The RFC treats it as one logical entity, even if it runs on several machines.

PPSTP does not move any media. It only says which peers can provide the content. The signaling between peers and the transfer of media data are out of scope, and PPSTP is not designed for applications that need in-sync reception.
sections.eli5: The tracker is like a class list. It does not hand out the video itself. It only tells each viewer which other viewers have pieces to share.

sections.title: A Typical Session
sections.content:
A viewer's Client Media Player first visits a service portal and picks content. The portal returns a Media Presentation Description (MPD) that names one or more trackers for the swarm that carries that content. A swarm is the group of peers exchanging chunks of the same content.

The local peer then sends a CONNECT to the tracker to join the swarm, and the tracker answers with an OK and a peer list. After that, chunk requests go from peer to peer using a peer protocol such as RFC 7574. While connected, the peer reports status with STAT_REPORT, and asks for a fresh list with FIND when it needs to refresh its neighborhood, for example because of churn.

Peers act in one of two modes. A LEECH downloads content and also shares what it has. A SEEDER only contributes content, and joins with complete media content. A peer must first get a peer ID, and any security certificates or tokens, from an enrollment service. The peer ID must be unique.
sections.eli5: You pick a show, the tracker gives you a list of friends who have pieces, and then you trade pieces with them. You check in now and then so the tracker knows you are still there.

sections.title: Layers and Messaging Model
sections.content:
PPSTP has three layers: a request/response layer, a message layer and a transport layer. The messaging model follows HTTP, currently version 1.1 in RFC 7230, and the RFC says PPSTP is meant to support future HTTP versions too.

The design is REST-like, so that existing HTTP implementations and infrastructure can be reused. Messages use UTF-8. Requests go from peers to the tracker, and the tracker sends a single response to each request. PPSTP uses the HTTP POST method, with parameters encoded as JSON in the body.

Implementations MUST support the https URI scheme and TLS. The media type for all PPSTP request parameters and responses is application/ppsp-tracker+json. Where the tracker wants to authenticate peers, HTTP Digest Access Authentication (RFC 7616) MUST be supported, with TLS client authentication preferred if available.
sections.eli5: PPSTP is built from ordinary web parts. A peer sends a note in a standard web envelope, and the tracker sends one note back.

sections.title: Tracker State Machines
sections.content:
The tracker itself has a very simple state machine. It sits in INIT when no peers are connected, moves to STARTED when the first peer registers, and stays there while at least one peer ID is registered. When the last one is removed it goes to TERMINATED, which is transient and returns straight to INIT.

Each registered peer ID also gets its own state machine. A CONNECT from a new peer ID starts it, registers the peer and starts an init timer. If the swarm actions succeed, the tracker stops the init timer, starts a track timer and answers. In the TRACKING state, a STAT_REPORT or FIND resets the track timer, and so does a valid CONNECT.

Things go wrong in a few ways. A CONNECT with only invalid swarm actions, or a request from an unregistered or invalid peer ID, makes the tracker answer with an error, delete the registration and destroy the state machine. If the track timer expires with no messages, the tracker cleans up all information about the peer in every swarm it joined. The RFC notes these cases may be peer malfunctions or malicious behavior, so ending the state machine is a preventive measure.
sections.eli5: The tracker keeps a stopwatch for each viewer. If you keep checking in, the stopwatch resets. If you go quiet too long, you are crossed off the list.

sections.title: Message and Element Formats
sections.content:
Every message has a root field named PPSPTrackerProtocol holding either a request or a response. The RFC defines its fields in a C-style notation similar to the one used for TLS, with JSON underneath.

A request carries version, request_type, transaction_id, peer_id and the request data. The version MUST be present and the only defined value is 1; 0 is reserved. A response carries version, response_type, error_code, transaction_id, and optionally the requester's public address (peer_addr) and one or more swarm_result elements. The response type is 0 for successful and 1 for failed.

Several building blocks recur:

  • Swarm action: a swarm_id, an action of JOIN or LEAVE, and a peer_mode of SEEDER or LEECH.
  • Peer number: peer_count, the maximum number of peers wanted in the returned list (it should be less than 30), plus optional hints ability_nat, concurrent_links, online_time and upload_bandwidth.
  • Peer address: IP address, port, priority and a type of HOST, REFLEXIVE or PROXY, with optional connection (wired or wireless), AS number and peer protocol.
  • Statistics: a STREAM_STATS block with swarm_id, uploaded_bytes, downloaded_bytes, available_bandwidth and concurrent_links.
sections.eli5: Every note uses the same form with boxes to fill in: who you are, what you want, and which group you mean. The tracker answers on a matching form.

sections.title: CONNECT, FIND and STAT_REPORT
sections.content:
CONNECT registers a peer and asks for swarm actions. A peer that already has the content and wants to share it sets JOIN with mode SEEDER. A peer that wants to consume content sets JOIN with mode LEECH. To leave a swarm it sets LEAVE. One request can hold several swarm actions, so a viewer switching channels can leave one swarm and join another in a single message. A table in the RFC lists which combinations of mode, action and state are valid. For a SEEDER or a LEECH the tracker adds the peer to the swarm, and for a LEECH it also builds a peer list that must contain peer IDs and IP addresses.

FIND asks for a new peer list for a swarm whenever needed. The tracker may weigh peer ability, how popular the content is, and network location. It may use hints such as ALTO, which the RFC says is out of scope. The response MUST include a peer group with peer IDs and addresses. If the request has no peer_num, the tracker may return a random sample of the peers.

STAT_REPORT is sent periodically while a peer is active. It carries statistics, but if it carries none it works as a keep-alive that stops the tracker from de-registering the peer when the track timer expires. Every response MUST use the same transaction_id as its request.

If a peer gets an invalid response, it MUST repeat the same request with identical content, including the same transaction_id. The tracker MUST be ready to receive a repeated transaction_id. Retry timing is left to the implementation. Implementations MUST ignore unknown members in a message body.
sections.eli5: There are only three things a viewer can say: 'let me in or out', 'who else can I get pieces from?', and 'I am still here, and here is how I am doing.'

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC lists threats common to open peer-to-peer systems: eavesdropping on signaling, forging or denying information about content, impersonating a valid participant and denial-of-service attacks on a chosen victim. It says no security system can guarantee complete security when participants may be malicious or uncooperative.

TLS MUST be used between peers and the tracker for privacy and data integrity. Messages received by the tracker SHOULD come from authorized peers, who SHOULD enroll through a centralized enrollment server that supplies a peer ID and authentication information. The enrollment method itself is out of scope. OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) with a bearer token is suggested as a way to add authentication.

Malicious peers may claim to own popular content and serve polluted data. The RFC points to the Merkle hash tree integrity protection in the peer protocol (RFC 7574) for detecting this, and admits there is no standard way for peers to completely avoid false peer lists from a bad tracker. To blunt Sybil attacks, the enrollment server SHOULD carefully regulate the rate of peer and tracker admission.

Peers send IP addresses and ports to the tracker, so anyone who can read those messages can study peer behavior. PPSTP does not rely on HTTP cookies, so a peer may decline to return cookies it receives from the tracker to make tracking harder.
sections.eli5: Some viewers might lie or sneak a bad piece into the pile. So the tracker asks to see ID cards first, and everybody talks through a locked tube so nobody can listen in.

sections.title: Extending PPSTP
sections.content:
An extension MUST NOT alter an existing protocol schema, because that would create a new version rather than an extension. Extensions MUST be documented in Standards Track RFCs if there are requirements for coordination, interoperability and broad distribution.

Two forms are allowed. A Request-Response Extension adds elements or attributes to an existing element, such as extra fields in the statistics block, and should be tried first. A Protocol-Level Extension defines new requests and responses. The RFC gives an illustration of a version with JOIN and DISCONNECT messages.

Extensions MUST be backward compatible with the base protocol and clearly define their semantics. New method names SHOULD be in capitals and shorter than 16 characters. IANA keeps registries for version numbers, request types and error codes, and new entries need IETF Review. The RFC also registers the media type application/ppsp-tracker+json.
sections.eli5: If you want to add a new move to the game, you may add a bit to an existing one or make a new one. But the old rules have to keep working for everyone.
